episode_title: Everyone Is Still Undersizing the AI Market | Eric Vishria

real_qa.q: Why does Fireworks achieve 5x performance difference compared to cloud providers running the same open source models on identical NVIDIA hardware?
real_qa.r: Running large language models efficiently is extremely hard. Fireworks achieves 5x performance speed and multiple times throughput difference compared to cloud providers like AWS, Azure, and GCP running the same open source models on the same NVIDIA hardware because these cloud companies pay cloud provider margins on top while Fireworks has specialized expertise in running these models efficiently. The key insight is that these companies are paying the margins of the cloud providers and running on top, making money—showing this is not a commodity pass-through business but requires deep technical expertise.

real_qa.q: What did AWS investor sentiment reveal about predicting long-term margin sustainability in infrastructure businesses in 2007?
real_qa.r: In 2007, when Bezos first discussed AWS in his annual letter after S3 and EC2 launched in 2006, the investor reaction was poor. If you put 30 of the smartest investors at that time in a room and asked them the probability that AWS would be a good business with durable long-term margins, Vishria estimates you would have gotten zero for 30 correct answers, even among really smart people who were around at that time.

real_qa.q: How did the market size for cloud infrastructure prove wrong the 2014 narrative that AWS would consume all enterprise software opportunities?
real_qa.r: By 2014, the prevailing narrative was that AWS would eat everything including databases, infrastructure, and applications due to its ability to offer services at 8% gross margin versus SaaS companies running at 85% gross margins. However, the market was so large that one vendor could not scale and consume it all. Instead, you saw Snowflake outperform Amazon Redshift, Datadog become a $100 billion company competing against AWS monitoring tools, plus Confluent, Elastic, Mongo, and Databricks all succeed. Additionally, Azure and GCP became unbelievable businesses, creating an oligopoly that now appears to be roughly 40-30-20 split, with smaller players like Cloudflare emerging as another $100 billion company.
real_qa.requete: AWS 2014 narrative enterprise software Snowflake Datadog

real_qa.q: What does the comparison between cloud adoption timelines and current AI adoption reveal about enterprise readiness in 2025?
real_qa.r: In 2010-2014, enterprises were super skeptical of cloud until they realized adoption was becoming a recruiting and competitive necessity. By contrast, today's enterprises are not dismissive about AI—they want it, are running experiments, spending against it, and view it as both more of an opportunity and more of a threat than they initially viewed cloud. They view AI as having more potential impact on their business, likely because they learned lessons from missing cloud adoption.

real_qa.q: How do product managers and engineers need to work differently in the AI era compared to traditional SaaS product development?
real_qa.r: In traditional product management, product managers understood customer problems but didn't specify implementation—that was the engineer's job. In the AI era, you must understand the jagged edge of model capabilities (what they're great at and where they fail), understand the customer problem, and bridge those gaps to build valuable solutions. You cannot do traditional product management anymore; you actually need to understand the nuances of model capabilities and put them together with customer problems. This mirrors how Cursor evolved from IDE to Tab Autocomplete to Agentic work, constantly iterating as the edge of capabilities changed.
real_qa.requete: AI product management jagged edge capabilities

real_qa.q: Why does hitting a SaaS plan destroy equity value in the AI era when it previously created it?
real_qa.r: For decades, the playbook was to lay out a plan, execute against it relentlessly and violently, hit your plan, and build equity value. But now the competitive frontier has completely shifted. Every day you hit that plan, you are destroying equity value because you should be pivoting toward AI opportunities. SaaS companies trading at 3x revenue today (down from 30x in 2021) are worth less even though they've grown 4x in a few years, gotten to breakeven, and hit their plans—because they haven't shifted toward what actually creates value now.
real_qa.requete: SaaS hitting plan destroying value AI

guest.bio_context: Eric Vishria is a venture investor at Sequoia Capital who joined the venture business in 2014. He has deep expertise in cloud infrastructure and SaaS businesses, having invested in and learned from companies like Sierra and Fireworks. He brings experience evaluating how new technology platforms get adopted by enterprises and how competitive dynamics shift as technology substrates change.
